name: Why did China keep reuniting while Europe stayed divided?

positions.claim: China faced one overwhelming threat, horse nomads on its northern frontier, and only a large centralised state could meet it; Europe faced many smaller threats from all sides.
positions.mech: A single threat direction rewards size and centralisation; scattered threats reward local defence and fragmentation. Steppe pressure also bred conquest regimes (Sui-Tang, Yuan, Qing) that rebuilt the empire from the north.
for: Nearly every reunification came from the north, and most by regimes with steppe or frontier roots.
Ko, Koyama and Sng's model matches when Chinese capitals and walls sat near the frontier.
Turchin finds mega-empires cluster on the steppe edge across Eurasia.
against: Europe also faced steppe invaders (Huns, Avars, Magyars, Mongols) without unifying.
The Song unified the south and north without a steppe origin, and lost the north to steppe regimes anyway.

positions.claim: China has one huge fertile core, the North China Plain joined to the Yangzi, with no internal barriers; Europe is cut by mountains, peninsulas and seas into defensible pieces.
positions.mech: Whoever holds a large open core outproduces and outfights everyone else and snowballs; mountain-ringed cores survive conquest.
for: Simulations on real terrain and soil maps unify China and fragment Europe without any cultural input.
European states that lasted (France, Spain, England) sit in natural compartments.
against: Geography is fixed but China was divided for long stretches (220-589, 907-1279).
The Alps did not stop Rome.

positions.school: The idea of Great Unity and the bureaucracy
positions.claim: Since Qin and Han, Chinese political culture recognised only one legitimate ruler of All-under-Heaven, and the examination bureaucracy gave elites a stake in serving him.
positions.mech: Elites saw division as abnormal, so every regional strongman aimed at the whole; a portable bureaucratic template let conquerors rebuild the state quickly.
for: No Chinese regime between 220 and 1683 claimed to be a permanent separate state in the way European kingdoms did.
Conquest dynasties (Yuan, Qing) adopted the bureaucracy and the examinations.
against: Ideology does not raise armies: the unifiers were usually frontier warlords.
Christendom also had a universal ideal (the Empire, the Papacy) that never unified Europe.

positions.school: Self-strengthening beat the balance of power
positions.claim: In the Warring States, Qin's ruthless reforms overcame the balancing that kept Europe plural; that victory set the template of universal empire for later China.
positions.mech: Mass conscription and direct taxation let one state outgrow rivals faster than coalitions could form.
for: Close parallels between early modern European and Warring States military-fiscal reforms.
against: Explains the first unification (221 BCE) better than the later ones after 600.

positions.claim: After the Tang aristocracy was destroyed, China's elites were fragmented local lineages that could not challenge the throne: the empire was durable because society was too divided to resist it, but weak because it could not tax.
positions.mech: A 'sandglass' elite network lets the ruler survive but traps the state in low capacity.
for: Epitaph evidence shows the great clans' destruction in the 880s; Song elites' kin networks were local.
against: Network data are thin before the Song; the logic struggles to explain conquest regimes.

state: Most economic historians now combine the steppe-threat and geography arguments (Scheidel's synthesis); the ideological account is accepted as a reinforcing factor rather than a first cause. Europe's fragmentation is increasingly seen as the precondition, not the cause, of its later growth.
settle: Comparative cases: does unification track steppe pressure in India, Iran and Russia? Better data on when Chinese regional regimes actually tried to stay independent, and spatial models that add the steppe to the fractured-land simulations.
fun: Rome never came back; the Chinese empire came back five times. Was it the horses, the mountains, or an idea?

name: When did Western Europe actually become richer than China?

positions.claim: China's GDP per head hovered around Song levels for seven centuries while Italy, Holland and Britain pulled ahead by 1400; after 1700 China's fell outright, so the gap predates industry by centuries.
positions.mech: Rebuilt national accounts from Song, Ming and Qing data on land, yields, crafts and population show output per head falling as population grew.
for: Maddison 2020 series: China about 1,225 (2011 dollars) in 1000, 1,404 in 1400, 1,543 in 1700 and 858 in 1850; Britain 1,717 in 1400 and 3,343 in 1800.
Allen et al. find 18th-century Chinese real wages near bare subsistence, far below London's.
against: Song and Ming data are thin and the population figures behind 'per head' are disputed.
Whole-country averages compare a continent-sized China with small rich regions of Europe.

positions.claim: The Yangzi delta and England were broadly comparable in living standards and markets until the late 1700s; the gap opened with coal and colonies.
positions.mech: Both cores hit ecological limits; England escaped through coal near its cities and land-intensive goods from the Americas, Jiangnan did not.
for: Comparable life expectancy, consumption of sugar and cloth, and market integration in the 18th-century delta.
Li Bozhong's Jiangnan farm productivity rose until 1850.
against: Allen et al. and Li-van Zanden find delta incomes well below England's by 1800.
Coal existed in north China; the problem was not only geology.

positions.claim: Comparing like with like, the Yangzi delta matched southern Europe but fell well behind the North Sea economies during the 1600s-1700s.
positions.mech: Real wage baskets and a regional national account place the delta in the 1820s at about half the Netherlands' GDP per head.
for: Beijing and Canton welfare ratios resemble Milan's, not London's.
Huating-Lou national accounts, 1820s.
against: Regional sources are few; wages of unskilled urban workers may misstate peasant household incomes.

positions.claim: The gap came from property relations, state capacity and culture: English agrarian capitalism and a strong fiscal-military state versus Chinese household involution and a light-touch empire.
positions.mech: Market compulsion forced English farms to raise labour productivity; Qing low taxes left little for infrastructure or protection of trade.
for: Britain taxed several times more per head than the Qing in the 18th century.
Delta output per day of labour stagnated while per acre rose.
against: Hard to measure property security comparably; Qing markets were free by many measures.

positions.claim: Ming-Qing wage and price evidence is too sparse and unrepresentative to support any precise date for the divergence.
positions.mech: Source criticism of the handful of wage series used in every comparison.
for: Many Chinese wage figures come from a few official construction and handicraft regulations.
against: National accounts triangulate from many sources beyond wages.

state: Since Broadberry, Guan and Li (2018) and the Maddison 2020 update, most economic historians accept an early divergence at the national level (China behind Britain and Holland by about 1400-1500), while the California school's narrower claim about the richest regions has been pushed back to around 1700 rather than 1800. The causes of the later, much larger gap (coal, colonies, institutions) are still argued.
settle: Better Ming and early Qing population and output data, more regional wage series from Chinese archives, and agreed price deflators for converting Song and Ming money values.
fun: In 1000 a Song farmer was about as rich as an Englishman; by 1850 the Englishman earned five times as much. Where did China's lead go, and when?

name: Was there a Song industrial revolution, and why did it stall?

positions.claim: Northern Song iron and coal output reached levels Europe would only see in the 18th century; the boom was killed by war and the loss of the north, not by any inner limit.
positions.mech: Deforestation pushed smelters to coal and coke; demand from the army and capital drove scale.
for: About 125,000 tons of iron in 1078, a sixfold rise since 806.
Coal-fired iron works in Hebei and Shandong.
against: The tonnage rests on tax quotas and is probably too high.
No sustained productivity growth followed even in the Southern Song, which kept the south.

positions.school: Economic revolution, then the high-level equilibrium trap
positions.claim: The Song had a real revolution in farming, water transport, money, markets and science; later China grew in size but not in technique as population filled the land.
positions.mech: Cheap labour and an already efficient technology killed the incentive to invent.
for: Shiba's catalogue of Song commercial institutions.
Few major inventions after 1350.
against: The trap is hard to test and ignores later Qing productivity gains in Jiangnan.

positions.school: Smithian growth driven by the fiscal state
positions.claim: Song growth was market expansion and specialisation (Smithian), pushed by a cash-hungry war state; it ended when the fiscal state changed, not because of a technological trap.
positions.mech: Military procurement and cash taxes monetised the economy; monopolies and conquest later reversed it.
for: Revenue and money supply track state spending.
The tea monopoly destroyed Sichuan's tea industry.
against: Underplays genuine technical change in rice, iron and printing.

positions.school: The Tang-Song transition began China's early modern age
positions.claim: Between Tang and Song, aristocratic rule gave way to autocracy plus a commoner examination elite and a commercial society: a social revolution, not just an economic one.
positions.mech: The end of the great clans opened office and markets to commoners.
for: Examination degree holders replace pedigree in office.
Urban wards and curfews vanish; markets spread into the countryside.
against: 'Early modern' imports a European template; much continuity in landholding.

state: Few now speak of a Song 'industrial revolution' in the British sense; the consensus, led by von Glahn and the national accountants, is of a remarkable Smithian boom that left Song China the richest economy of its time, with a GDP per head that China roughly held, but never durably surpassed, until its 18th-century decline. Hartwell's iron figures remain influential but are treated as upper bounds.
settle: Archaeometallurgy of Song iron sites to test Hartwell's tonnage; better price series from Song documents to separate output growth from monetisation.
fun: In 1078 China smelted more iron than all of Europe would until the 1700s. So why no steam engine in Kaifeng?

name: Why did modern science and industry not arise in China?

positions.claim: China's mandarin state encouraged useful technology but never let merchants or independent scholars gain the autonomy that joined craft knowledge to mathematics in Europe.
positions.mech: Social structure, not intellect: the state absorbed talent and capital.
for: Thirty volumes of Science and Civilisation in China document Chinese priority in many fields.
against: The Marxian category of 'bureaucratic feudalism' is loose; Europe's states were also bureaucratising.

positions.claim: Pre-modern invention came from experience and grew with population; the scientific method requires trained talent, which China's examinations steered into the classics.
positions.mech: Incentives: the highest returns were to memorising Neo-Confucian commentary for office.
for: Zhu Xi orthodoxy was the examination curriculum from 1313 to 1905.
against: Elman shows Qing scholars did serious mathematics and astronomy (evidential research).

positions.claim: A high-level equilibrium: so many people and so efficient a traditional economy that machines did not pay.
positions.mech: Relative prices: cheap labour, dear resources.
for: Simple machines like the water-powered spinning frame existed in Yuan China and were not developed.
against: Explains industry better than science.

positions.school: No market for ideas in a unified empire
positions.claim: Europe's many states and its autonomous universities and corporations let heterodox ideas survive and compete; China's single empire and orthodoxy did not.
positions.mech: Exit options for thinkers and legal autonomy for institutions of learning.
for: Galileo's and Descartes's work circulated across borders despite condemnation at home.
against: Chinese scholars also moved between patrons; Islamic science faced a plural world and still stalled.

positions.claim: Asking why something did not happen in China measures China by a European yardstick; Chinese science had its own aims and in the 17th century absorbed European astronomy readily.
positions.mech: Historiographical: counterfactual 'failure' questions misread the sources.
for: Jesuit astronomy was adopted at the Qing court; Chinese mathematics revived in the 18th century.
against: The divergence in technology by 1850 is a real fact that still needs explaining.

state: Historians of science mostly side with Sivin and Elman that 'failure' is a misleading frame; economic historians still ask the question in the form of the Great Divergence, where Elvin's relative-price argument and Mokyr's market for ideas are the live candidates.
settle: Systematic counts of inventions and their diffusion in China and Europe by period, and comparative studies of how scientific claims were tested and spread.
fun: Paper, print, gunpowder and the compass were Chinese. Newton was English. Needham spent fifty years asking why.

name: What caused the An Lushan rebellion, and did it really kill 36 million people?

positions.claim: Xuanzong's court handed huge standing armies to frontier generals and then let the chief minister Yang Guozhong try to destroy the strongest of them; An Lushan rebelled to save himself.
positions.mech: Militarised frontiers plus a factional court: the general's armies were bigger than anything the court controlled.
for: About 490,000 frontier troops by 742; An commanded three commands with some 180,000 men.
Yang Guozhong's accusations from 752.
against: Explains timing, not the decades of breakdown that followed.

positions.claim: The Tang were locked in an expensive multi-front competition with Tibet, the Turks, the Khitan and Nanzhao; professional frontier armies were a rational response that made a rebellion possible.
positions.mech: Imperial grand strategy in a crowded Inner Asian arena.
for: Disasters in Yunnan (751, 754) and at Talas (751) in the same years.
against: Other empires ran frontier armies without such a catastrophe.

positions.school: A registration collapse, not 36 million deaths
positions.claim: The fall from about 53 million to 17 million registered people mostly reflects the collapse of the state's ability to count, plus refugees and tax evaders, not deaths.
positions.mech: War destroyed the registers; the new property-based taxes after 780 no longer needed a head count.
for: Recovery to only about 9 million households by the 800s while the economy grew.
Whole provinces stopped reporting.
against: Real losses in the north China plain were very heavy; no-one can say how heavy.

positions.claim: Taken at face value, the registers record a loss of some 36 million people.
positions.mech: Literal reading of the census.
for: The fall in registered population is real and documented.
against: No demographer accepts the registers as a death count.

positions.school: The great turning point of Chinese history
positions.claim: Whatever its cause, the rebellion ended the cosmopolitan, aristocratic, land-allotting Tang order and began the shift to a commercial, southern, examination-run China.
positions.mech: Fiscal (salt and two-tax), demographic (south) and social (end of aristocracy) changes cascading over 150 years.
for: Salt monopoly from 758, two-tax 780, population moves south, aristocracy destroyed 880-907.
against: Many of these trends began before 755.

state: Pulleyblank's political account of the outbreak still frames the field, with Skaff and Graff adding the strategic context. Demographers agree the 36-million figure is a registration artefact; the internet's 'deadliest war in history' claim is a myth.
settle: Archaeological and regional evidence of settlement abandonment in Hebei and Henan in the 750s-760s, compared with the registers.
fun: A census that lost 36 million people in five years: the deadliest war in history, or the biggest paperwork failure?

name: What launched the Mongol conquests?

positions.school: A wet decade fuelled the war machine
positions.claim: Tree rings from lava-field pines show 1211-1225 was the wettest, mildest run in 1,112 years; abundant grass fed the horses and herds that powered expansion.
positions.mech: Grassland productivity converts directly into horses, livestock and political capital on the steppe.
for: Fifteen consecutive wet years coincide with the conquest of north China and Central Asia.
against: Correlation; the expansion began in 1209 and continued after the wet years ended.

positions.claim: Drought and hunger drove nomads to raid and conquer settled neighbours.
positions.mech: Push from failing pasture.
for: Severe drought in the 1180s preceded Temujin's rise.
against: The conquests coincide with a wet phase, not a dry one.

positions.claim: Temujin dismantled the old tribal order and rebuilt it as a decimal army bound to him, with merit promotion and a law code; climate was a background condition.
positions.mech: Organisation: loyal, disciplined, mobile units under a single command.
for: Units of ten to ten thousand mixed men from defeated tribes.
Polo describes exactly this command system.
against: Great leaders also emerged in dry periods without world conquest.

positions.school: A steppe state lives on plunder
positions.claim: A supratribal polity on the steppe has no tax base; it must keep conquering or extorting sedentary neighbours to reward its followers, or fall apart.
positions.mech: Redistribution of plunder holds the confederation together.
for: Steppe empires typically formed and collapsed with their access to Chinese wealth.
against: Does not explain why this confederation went far beyond extortion to direct rule.

state: Since 2014 the pluvial is widely cited as an enabling condition, folded into a political account that gives Chinggis's reorganisation of the tribes the lead role. The drought-push model is abandoned for this case.
settle: More tree-ring sites across the eastern steppe, and herd-size models that link grassland productivity to the size of armies.
fun: The wettest fifteen years in a millennium, right when the Mongols rode out: luck, fuel, or coincidence?

name: Why did the Ming fall in 1644?

positions.claim: A Ming economy and treasury dependent on imported silver was hit when Japanese and American supplies fell around 1639-44, raising the burden of silver taxes and debts in the worst harvest years.
positions.mech: Monetary contraction: dearer silver, falling grain prices for sellers, heavier real taxes.
for: Sakoku 1639, the 1639 Manila massacre and Spanish shipping losses.
Contemporary complaints about silver scarcity.
against: Von Glahn shows import volumes stayed high into the 1640s.

positions.school: The monetary crisis is a myth
positions.claim: Silver imports did not collapse in the 1640s and silver prices behaved in ways the crisis theory cannot explain; the Ming fell for domestic political and military reasons.
positions.mech: Data on imports and prices.
for: Revised import estimates high in the 1630s-40s.
Copper cash depreciated, contrary to a silver shortage.
against: Local scarcity may still have mattered where trade routes broke.

positions.school: Climate: the Little Ice Age's worst decade
positions.claim: The 1630s-40s were among the coldest and driest decades in China in two millennia; harvests failed for years, famine and epidemics followed, and rebellions grew into armies.
positions.mech: Cold and drought, worsened by eruptions in 1640-41, cut grain output while the state demanded more.
for: Documentary temperature reconstructions; gazetteer records of drought, locusts and famine 1627-1643.
Epidemics in Beijing 1643-44.
against: Climate hit Japan and Korea too, and their regimes survived.

positions.school: War with the Manchus broke the treasury
positions.claim: A rigid, low-yield fiscal system could not pay for the war in Liaodong; surtaxes and unpaid armies created the rebels the court then could not suppress.
positions.mech: Fiscal-military overstretch on two fronts.
for: Liaodong surtaxes from 1618; 1629 postal-system cuts that created Li Zicheng's army.
against: The Ming had survived costly wars before (the Imjin war in Korea, 1592-98).

positions.school: Rational rebels in a failing state
positions.claim: Rebellion broke out where state capacity to punish was weakest and hardship greatest: bandits made a calculation.
positions.mech: Rational-choice model of collective violence across the Ming.
for: County-level data on Ming rebellions.
against: Explains where rather than why in 1640s.

state: Parker and Brook's climate synthesis now dominates, combined with Swope's military-fiscal story; most accept von Glahn's critique of a pure silver-import crisis, while some, following Atwell, keep a role for silver scarcity in particular regions.
settle: Year-by-year silver import series reconciled across Japanese, Spanish and Chinese sources, and county-level matching of drought, epidemic and rebellion dates.
fun: Cold, drought, plague, a silver squeeze and a two-front war all hit Beijing in the same five years. Which one actually killed the Ming?

name: Why was the Taiping war so vast, and why did the Qing survive it?

positions.claim: Hong Xiuquan's visions, read through a Protestant tract, gave the movement its discipline, iconoclasm and total war against the 'Manchu demons'.
positions.mech: Religious conviction made compromise impossible and mobilised the marginal Hakka.
for: Taiping texts, rituals and the ban on opium, foot-binding and idols.
against: Faith explains the core, not the millions who joined for food and safety.

positions.claim: A tripled population with no land frontier, plus a silver drain that doubled the real tax burden, made the south ready to explode.
positions.mech: Malthusian and monetary stress on poor households.
for: Population near 430 million by 1850; copper-silver exchange rates doubled 1800-1850.
against: The rising began in Guangxi's specific ethnic conflicts, not in the most crowded regions.

positions.school: The Opium War broke the south
positions.claim: Defeat in 1842 discredited the dynasty, militarised the Guangdong countryside and threw porters and boatmen out of work as trade moved to Shanghai.
positions.mech: Social disorder in the trade's old hinterland.
for: Secret-society risings across Guangdong and Guangxi in the 1840s.
against: The Taiping core in Guangxi was far from Canton.

positions.school: Local elites and regional armies saved the Qing
positions.claim: The dynasty survived because gentry-led militia and Zeng Guofan's Xiang Army did what the banners could not; the price was a permanent shift of power to the provinces.
positions.mech: Militarisation of local society from the White Lotus to the Taiping.
for: The Xiang and Huai armies took Nanjing; lijin trade taxes paid them.
against: Underplays foreign help in the delta.

positions.school: A global civil war decided by Britain
positions.claim: Britain's switch from neutrality to intervention after 1860, to protect its Shanghai trade and the treaty settlement, tipped a balanced war to the Qing.
positions.mech: Foreign naval and mercenary force plus customs revenue.
for: Defence of Shanghai 1860-62; the Ever-Victorious Army.
against: Foreign troops were small; the decisive sieges were won by Chinese armies.

positions.school: A light state could not stop it
positions.claim: Qing taxation per head had fallen for a century; the state had too few officials and troops to stop a regional rising before it became a war.
positions.mech: Principal-agent limits in a huge empire kept the state thin.
for: Fixed tax quotas since 1712; small magistrate staffs.
against: The same state had crushed many earlier risings.

state: Kuhn's argument about regional militarisation remains the framework for the Qing survival; Platt has put the international dimension back in, and Meyer-Fong has shifted attention to the experience and memory of mass death. Most accounts combine Spence's religious core with Wakeman's social disorder and the economic stress described by Lin.
settle: County-level population reconstructions for 1850-1880, and archives on how lijin revenue and foreign customs funds were split between the provinces and Beijing.
fun: A failed exam candidate who believed he was Jesus's younger brother started a war that killed more people than the First World War.

name: Why did Japan industrialise first in East Asia?

positions.claim: Two centuries of peace built commercial farming, rural industry, literacy and an 'industrious revolution'; Meiji industry grew out of these native sources.
positions.mech: Skills, markets and work habits accumulated before 1868.
for: Rural by-employment and proto-industry; high male literacy by the 1860s.
against: China's Jiangnan had similar commercial depth and did not industrialise.

positions.school: A modernising state and late development
positions.claim: The Meiji state centralised revenue, built schools and railways and led a catch-up spurt with the newest technology.
positions.mech: State-led investment financed by a fixed land tax.
for: Land tax reform 1873; national schooling 1872; state railways and model factories.
against: Many state factories lost money and were sold off in the 1880s; private firms led growth.

positions.claim: Forced opening in 1859 moved Japan from near-autarky to free trade at once, yielding large gains from comparative advantage and a silk export boom.
positions.mech: Relative prices converged to world levels; resources shifted to silk and tea.
for: Price data from Osaka and Yokohama show silk and tea prices jumping toward world prices.
against: Gains were one-off; China was opened too.

positions.school: A capable centre versus a fragmented Qing
positions.claim: In the same silk industry, Japan's state and associations standardised and modernised while China's decentralised late Qing could not; the difference was political capacity.
positions.mech: Public goods (egg inspection, schools, credit) need a strong centre.
for: Japan overtook China in raw silk exports by about 1905.
against: Some Chinese regions (Shanghai, Guangdong) did modernise silk reeling.

positions.school: Japan was already pulling away slowly
positions.claim: Japanese GDP per head grew slowly from the 1720s while China's fell, so by 1850 Japan was ahead of China though far behind Britain.
positions.mech: Gradual Smithian growth under the Tokugawa.
for: Japan about 1,436 versus China 858 in 1850 (Maddison 2020, 2011 dollars).
against: The estimates rest on uncertain output and population data.

state: The field combines the Tokugawa-foundations view with the Meiji state's role; the national-accounting work of Bassino and colleagues now shows Japan's lead over China predating 1868.
settle: Comparable regional accounts for Japan and Jiangnan in the 1850s-1880s, and firm-level data on how Meiji factories recruited rural labour.
fun: Two Asian empires forced open by Western gunboats in the 1850s; within forty years one was building battleships and the other was losing to them.

name: Do droughts drive nomads to war?

positions.claim: Over two thousand years, years of low rainfall saw more nomadic attacks on China, and wet years more Chinese attacks on the steppe.
positions.mech: Drought hits pasture harder than farmland, so the relative gains from raiding rise.
for: Statistical association between precipitation reconstructions and recorded conflicts.
against: Recorded conflicts depend on Chinese chroniclers' attention.

positions.claim: The Mongol expansion came in a pluvial: abundance, not scarcity, gave steppe rulers the horses to conquer.
positions.mech: Energy from grass to horses to armies.
for: 1211-1225 pluvial.
against: One case; Bai and Kung's long-run pattern points the other way.

positions.claim: Long cold phases across the preindustrial world line up with war, famine and population decline, via food prices.
positions.mech: Cooling cuts harvests; scarcity brings conflict.
for: Cross-correlation of temperature reconstructions and war counts 1400-1900.
against: Aggregate correlations hide the political mechanisms.

positions.claim: Climate matters case by case: the Uyghur empire survived a drought lasting nearly seven decades, while a single wet spring helped turn the Mongols back from Hungary.
positions.mech: Political organisation and mobility buffer or amplify climate shocks.
for: Uyghur drought without collapse; Hungarian marshes in 1242.
against: Case studies resist generalisation.

positions.claim: Steppe war followed the cycle of Chinese dynasties and steppe succession politics; the Mongols left Hungary because Ogedei died.
positions.mech: Tribute, succession and alliance decide war and peace.
for: Steppe empires rise with unified China; Batu's withdrawal fits the succession crisis.
against: Ignores new high-resolution climate evidence.

state: No single rule survives: the field has moved from 'drought drives raids' to case studies in which climate shocks interact with steppe politics, sometimes as push, sometimes as fuel, sometimes as neither.
settle: More high-resolution tree-ring records for the eastern steppe matched to well-dated conflicts, and models of herd dynamics under drought and pluvial conditions.
fun: Drought made nomads raid China, rain made them conquer the world, and seventy years of drought did nothing at all. What is going on?
